topic: Same MCP server, different answers: what the Harness measured
thesis: The same MCP server hands different harnesses different answers, so the measured compatibility table, not the protocol document, is the spec your agent actually implements.
explanation_path: MCP promised one protocol so any client could call any server, but a tool result arrives in two shapes, a text field and a structuredContent field, and the specification only says servers SHOULD mirror one into the other. That SHOULD is the crack the harnesses fall through: each agent app decides for itself whether the model sees the text, the structured object, both, or nothing. Grasp the double payload before the verdicts, because every result in the field guide comes from planting distinct random markers in the two fields and asking the agent what it can see. With the mechanism clear, the measured table lands as evidence rather than trivia: identical probes, named clients, pinned versions, different outcomes. The protocol-version split deepens the point, since the same server negotiated 2025-06-18 with Codex CLI and 2026-07-28 with Claude Code CLI, and the 2026 revision changed the connection handshake itself. The payoff for someone wiring tools locally: treat the compatibility table the way web developers once treated browser tables, as the working spec, and probe your own harness before you trust it.

claims.claim: What the Harness? went up as a Show HN post by Polytomic on 2026-10-20, framed around LLM agents (Claude, Codex, Grok, Amp, etc) being inconsistent in their MCP implementations, with tables inspired by the browser-compatibility tables of yore.
claims.source_title: Show HN: What the Harness? LLM agent inconsistencies in MCP implementation | Hacker News

claims.claim: The guide publishes the latest approved run per harness with the MCP client and version named, and its authors state that preferring one structured payload is a preference, not a claim about what the MCP standard mandates.
claims.source_title: What the Harness? · MCP compatibility field guide by Polytomic

claims.claim: On the double-payload probe, where one tool result carries both a text field and a structuredContent field, Claude Code CLI (MCP client version 2.1.296, run Oct 13, 2026) earned Pass: uses structured output, while Grok CLI (MCP client version 1.0.60, run Oct 19, 2026) earned Fail: Duplicate output, the same fail across 3 observed versions.
claims.source_title: What the Harness? · MCP compatibility field guide by Polytomic

claims.claim: When the probe returned structuredContent only, Grok Bot (MCP client version 0.1.0) and Cursor Agent CLI recorded Fail: No output, so the structured payload never surfaced to the agent.
claims.source_title: What the Harness? · MCP compatibility field guide by Polytomic

claims.claim: Connected to the same server, Claude Code CLI and Grok CLI negotiated protocol 2026-07-28 while Codex CLI (MCP client version 0.162.1) and Amp CLI negotiated 2025-06-18, and Cursor Desktop and Grok Bot negotiated 2025-11-25.
claims.source_title: What the Harness? · MCP compatibility field guide by Polytomic

claims.claim: The MCP specification for 2025-06-18 says that for backwards compatibility a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block, a SHOULD that leaves each harness free to pass one or both shapes to the model.

Version negotiation is built into MCP: if the server supports the requested protocol version it MUST respond with the same version, otherwise it MUST respond with another protocol version it supports, which is how one server ends up speaking three different versions to different clients.

The 2026-07-28 revision made MCP stateless by removing the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake, removed ping, and added a server/discover RPC, so the protocol a harness implements is a moving target.
MCP was created at Anthropic by David Soria Parra and Justin Spahr-Summers and introduced as a new standard for connecting AI assistants to the systems where data lives.
claims.source_title: Introducing the Model Context Protocol \ Anthropic

claims.claim: The probes plant independent random markers in content[0].text and structuredContent so an agent cannot infer an unseen marker from the other field, and the site states that exact token overhead was not measured.
claims.source_title: Run the probe · What the harness?

analogy_candidates.vehicle: Browser compatibility tables of the old web
analogy_candidates.mapping: the same web page rendered differently in each browser, so developers learned to test against measured compatibility grids instead of the W3C spec; the same MCP server now answers differently per harness, so you test against this grid
analogy_candidates.limit: browser quirks were mostly bugs against a fixed spec, while here the MCP spec itself only says SHOULD for mirroring structured output into text, so some of the measured divergence is legal behavior rather than a defect

misconceptions.myth: MCP is a standard, so plugging the same server into any agent gives the model the same tool output.
misconceptions.reality: the spec only says servers SHOULD mirror structured JSON into text, and measured runs show Claude Code CLI passing where Grok CLI duplicates and Grok Bot and Cursor Agent CLI drop the structured payload entirely (claims 3 and 4).

misconceptions.myth: Everyone speaks current MCP, so protocol version is a detail.
misconceptions.reality: against one server on runs dated Oct 5 to Oct 19, 2026, Claude Code CLI and Grok CLI negotiated 2026-07-28 while Codex CLI and Amp CLI sat on 2025-06-18 and Cursor and Grok Bot on 2025-11-25 (claims 5 and 8).

glossary.definition: An open protocol that lets an AI application call tools and read data exposed by a server over one standard connection.
The agent application that hosts the model and connects to MCP servers on its behalf, such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, or Grok CLI.
The JSON object field of a tool result, meant to carry machine-readable data.
The text portion of a tool result; the spec says servers SHOULD also mirror structured JSON here for backwards compatibility.
A tool result that ships the same data in both the text and structured fields, risking the model seeing it twice.
The dated revision of MCP a connection agrees to use, such as 2025-06-18 or 2026-07-28.
The rule that the server must answer with the client's requested protocol version if it supports it, otherwise another version it supports.
A grid of clients versus features showing what actually works where, in the tradition of the old browser-support tables.

unverified: How many tokens the duplicate payloads actually waste is unknown; the site's authors state exact token overhead was not measured.
Whether duplicated or dropped tool output measurably degrades agent accuracy on real tasks was not tested by anyone fetched this run.
Why Grok CLI still duplicates output across 3 observed versions while on the newest protocol has no stated cause; the site says a missing marker alone does not establish the cause.
How the Grok, OpenAI, and Cursor clients behave on versions newer than the latest observed runs (Oct 19, 2026) is unknown from these pages.
suggested_outline:
Cold open on the head-to-head: one server, one probe, Claude Code CLI at MCP client version 2.1.296 passes with structured output while Grok CLI at MCP client version 1.0.60 fails by duplicating the payload, the same fail across 3 observed versions.
The why: a tool result has two shapes and the spec only says SHOULD for mirroring one into the other, and the same server negotiates three different protocol versions to different clients, so the harness, not the server, decides what the model sees.
The payoff: the compatibility table is the working spec; carry the site's own hedge that its rubric is a preference rather than a mandate, then point your own harness at the public probe endpoint and see what your stack actually passes through.
notes: The run-history page (history.html) renders its data with client-side JavaScript and returned an empty shell when fetched, so per-run evidence pages were not individually readable; every verdict above comes from the main results tables. Do not blur the Grok entries: Grok CLI duplicates output while on the newest protocol (2026-07-28), whereas Grok Bot drops structured-only output while on 2025-11-25; they are different MCP clients (grok-shell-what-the-harness versus connectors-manager). The Hacker News post had 1 point and 0 comments at fetch time, so community reaction is not a load-bearing element.
viewer_situation: You run the same MCP server inside two different agents on your own machine and assume both harnesses show the model the same tool output.
process_steps: Add https://what-the-harness.polytomic.com/mcp as a Streamable HTTP MCP server in your agent's MCP settings.
Give your agent the site's test prompt so it begins a run and calls the three output probes.
Read the two test resources through MCP, not a browser, and record the exact markers you can see.
Submit the report with the markers, keep your run token private, and wait for review; the table then shows your harness's latest approved run.
objection: One probe server with reviewed community submissions is not a standards conformance suite, and each verdict describes a single recorded client version and session rather than the whole harness.
